reviews.review:
The first person I investigated was a lady with short blue hair, so I sent her to jail immediately.

Edit: So the actual game is way more limited than you might think, and also failed to convince me why the surveillance system is bad. I've not completed the final chapter because at this point I have to either willingly submit misinformation, or side with actual terrorists.

A great premise that certainly gets you invested, with certain pieces of information you choose to upload affecting the outcome. Whether that's for better or for worse - that's kind of up to you to decide which side of the fence you fall on. The game leaves it very ambiguous about which side is better - the agency you work for, or the people you are surveilling. Tapping phone calls and trawling social media pages lead seamlessly into conflicting news articles into further conflicting text messages - leaving you unsure what to trust as you decide what you should and shouldn't upload in the mismatch of information (because like House says, "People lie", right?)

Some areas are a little point and click, and the call & text dialogue could definitely do with a skip through feature for fast readers. However the story is very immersive and genuinely does have you wondering if you made the right choice. There are three possible endings, but also a number of outcomes for the characters within that based off your decisions.

A solid game (as is its sequel) for the price of ~£7 that has you questioning the price of surveillance for safety.

Clean and nicely cut is what comes to mind when playing this game.

The story is nicely written and so are the different interaction the character have. 

I would say that if you like social "investigations" and have few hours to spare you will not be disappointed.

I love the idea of being the brains/background detective behind the screen. It's like working from home, except I do feel some kind of way that there is only one case per game, and I'm going to have to download the game's sequel to continue playing this game. Though, the fact that this game has more than one ending is lovely.

The way the game has 4th wall breaks is quite lovely, and the way you are truly logging in to a job is quite fantastically new to me, and I love it. Don't speak to me of GTA and it's role-playing jobs, I mean where the job itself in the game is sitting behind a screen. Great stuff.
More a story than a game. End is frustrating, morale is a bit childish. But it was kind of nice to read through

I liked it. If you like games like 'The Roottrees are Dead' you'll probably like this too. Love games where you dig into documents and piece together profiles on people, map out relationships, timelines, etc. There's a fair amount of content as well which I liked.

My only issues with it (no story spoilers):
[list]
[*]It's a little... handholdey. It marks all documents/etc in your doc view that have outstanding clues, then highlights those clues inside the docs. So for big sections of the game you can just switch your brain off, click the marked docs, scroll down until you see a clue and action it. It doesn't entirely ruin things but I wish there was a way to switch it off
[*]It brings in the concept of junk 'clues' you have to sift through. Sometimes this is done well - someone has a picture of a dog as their profile picture, it's pretty safe to assume you don't need to add that to their file. But sometimes it gets a little nebulous - people's likes and dislikes for example. Maybe if someone says they don't like watching movies, then later someone was like 'I watched a movie with them' it would be helpful? Instead you just get snark from your supervisor for having the balls to pollute the file
[*]For the conflicting info, I wish it was possible to change your mind - I added the wrong info for someone at some point, immediately realised it was wrong, couldn't do anything about it, and then it got acted on. They explain it in the game as 'once you submit the info it immediately gets sent out' which is fine, but I feel like they would be less annoyed by me 'immediately sending out' an update than acting on false info
[/list]

A solid 7-8 out of 10 for me. Not perfect, but will def be picking up the second one.
Very fun and thought provoking. Great OSINT simulator that at the same time highlights it's weeknesses, which is rare in tech centered circles.

5 years passed. I decided to restart the game since I had forgotten most of the story anyway. I kid you not, played until the end of the same flipping chapter again and called it a day...

See you around in 2030, folks!

pretty disappointed at how limited the game is. it doesn't seem like it really wants you to read and make choices. you just open documents and select pre-highlighted phrases. i thought this would go away after doing the first day/tutorial but it didn't. i wanted to add stuff i was finding while reading different pages of websites, identifying patterns, etc. but it wasn't interact-able. i couldn't move photos to certain profiles when identified photos of them on the schools website or add info about their jobs. it really only let me pick out what it wanted me to, the game didn't really let me think for myself. obviously haven't completed it fully but given that a lot of the other reviews mention the game is centered on this first case and fairly short i'm really not interested after the first couple of days.

Great game

This was a really good game! I enjoyed the whole mystery of it all -- started out feeling like a murder mystery-type thing before the cards were turned on me real quick. Loved it!

Excellent short story-driven, investigative game. Finished it three times (there are three different endings) and got all achievements. And I was having blast the whole time!

In Orwell, it's your job as a government agent to spy on the lives of civilians and find out who is responsible for recent bombing attacks. The game touches on some pretty relevant topics today regarding cybersecurity.

So.. this game is most definitely what I'd call a hidden gem. Your choices have real consequences, and it's not as simple as dragging data chunks. Deciding which information to send or discard will seriously impact what happens. The gameplay does exactly what it aims to do, make you feel like a government agent. I'm a sucker for political/government simulators like this, so I really enjoyed it.

The story is brilliant. It's up to you to discover all that you can about the various characters. You'll find yourself liking some, hating some, and sympathizing with some despite their wrongdoings. This is definitely a game that challenges the player morally. The worldbuilding is super good. I found myself becoming super immersed while playing (so much so that I actually completed it one sitting and stayed up until about 1 am to complete it.)

Graphics are nice and the art style successfully gives off the Orwellian vibes. I don't quite know how to explain it but it definitely feels dystopian in a way. Well done.

The soundtrack mainly stays the same, but will become suspenseful or panicked when something goes wrong or when new, crucial information is discovered, which I really liked. I do think it would have been cool if the phone calls had voice actors rather than just text.

If you want something very different from most games, I'd highly recommend Orwell. I've already started playing the sequel.

Fast-paced in-depth story with addictive game mechanics. Also just the right length to leave a lasting impression (thank goodness there's a sequel bc I would be sad otherwise lol). Great fun, especially if you're looking for a bite-sized experience that doesn't feel shallow.
Very nice

Orwell is like stepping into the shoes of Big Brother but with just enough moral weight to make you squirm. You play as an investigator digging through people’s private lives, piecing together data from emails, chats, social media, and files to track down potential threats. Sounds chill, right? Yeah... until you realize every decision you make can mess up someone’s life, or worse.

The gameplay isn’t flashy, but that’s the point. It’s all about choices, judgment, and how far you're willing to go in the name of "security". The tension ramps up fast, and the story keeps you guessing with twists that'll have you second-guessing every click.

It’s part puzzle, part thriller, and part uncomfortable reflection on surveillance and privacy. If you like narrative-driven games that make you think (and sometimes feel a little dirty), Orwell is absolutely worth diving into. Just remember: someone’s always watching. And this time... it's you.

I liked this! But it's not without its issues. If I could give a neutral rating I would, but for now it's not bad enough for me to not recommend giving it a go, especially if it's on sale.

Overall the game was enjoyable and I liked getting to read through all of the documents and web pages. The story was also interesting. If you like narrative-heavy games, you'll probably enjoy this. 

Now, what I didn't like:

- Some of the information I submitted was counted as 'not relevant', but it feels unrealistic that this information wouldn't be relevant. For example, finding out that two characters who might be collaborating used to be a couple and have since broken up. I would say that's pretty important! I did enjoy some of this mechanic, such as characters obviously being sarcastic with each other, so you don't just add every bit of information you see.

- There's no hint button so if you get stuck, you have to resort to looking at a walkthrough.

- There's no way to skip through phone calls or text conversations and just read the transcript at the end. The final chapter has a verrrrry long phone call with an ending-deciding choice afterwards, and if you want to replay the final day and unlock the other endings you have to sit through the whole thing again. If these calls were voice acted I wouldn't mind, but you're just watching text appear onscreen at its own pace for what feels like forever.
If you're a data junkie, have a tendency to want to cyber-stalk people online, and enjoy playing morally ambiguous roles in games, then this is the game for you. Very engaging.

I love the game mechanics!

However, I wish the game gave players more power to decide what actions to take.

Since you’re just an information collector, the only way to influence the outcome is by choosing not to feed certain information to your supervisor. That limits a lot of freedom because you can't really control what a scripted supervisor thinks. And sometimes, if you don’t feed the plot-required information, the game just stops and waits for you, forcing you to still somewhat follow the intended plot. The illusion of "choice matter" in this case is worse than reading a visual novel.

Great singleplayer game! It's a good casual story telling game. Games like this are unique. Not whole lot of games out there that are like this. The gameplay, while very simple, is unique. 

The story is very straight forward. This game is perfect for people who are new to gaming in general. Very simple mechanics and nothing too complicated. 

I highly recommend it for casual players and players that enjoy singleplayer games!

Playing Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You was one of the most gripping and thought-provoking gaming experiences I’ve had in a while. I was immediately drawn into its investigative gameplay, where I took on the role of a government operative sifting through personal data to uncover potential threats. The way the narrative unfolded—layer by layer, twist by twist—kept me hooked from start to finish. What really stood out to me were the moral dilemmas: every decision I made felt weighty, and I constantly questioned whether I was protecting the public or infringing on personal freedoms. It was unsettling in the best way possible.

The mechanics were refreshingly intuitive, making it easy to dive right into the story without getting bogged down by complicated controls. Dragging and dropping data chunks, cross-referencing information, and piecing together the truth felt natural and satisfying. It’s a game that doesn’t just entertain—it makes you think. I had a blast playing it and would absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys narrative-driven games with a sharp edge of social commentary.

It is best to go into this game blind and make your choices based on your instinct.
The story is immersive and the gameplay, though simplistic, is immersive and enjoyable. 
You will likely agonize over some of your choices and look forward to the next twist and turn. It is a great story and definitely worth a buy.

[h1]Smart, subtle, and shockingly good: this one lingers long after the credits.[/h1]

Ever wondered what it would feel like to be Big Brother’s favorite intern? Orwell hands you the surveillance keys to a digital dystopia and asks: how far is too far when safety is on the line? Presented through simulated internet searches, social media sleuthing, and a stripped-down but powerful interface, this game is one of the most immersive narrative experiences I’ve played!

The choices are yours: what do you report? What gets ignored? You might think you're just dragging datachunks into files, but your decisions have real consequences, shaping a gripping narrative with multiple endings and gray-area morality at every turn. It’s as if Papers Please had a love child with 1984 and that baby learned to code.

There is a catch though : this isn't really a “puzzle” game despite the label (it’s more like an interactive spy-thriller/visual novel hybrid with branching paths and big philosophical questions). That said, I devoured it across three playthroughs to 100% the game and would gladly do more. Whether you’re a dystopia enthusiast or just looking for a smart, haunting slow burn, Orwell belongs on your must-play list, especially when it goes on sale (but even at full price, it’s a steal with around 4 hours of game play per playthrough).

P.-S. Stop reading about this masterpiece and go play it yourself. You'll thank me later for stopping you from reading too much. Going in blind is the best way to enjoy it!

[h1]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, all branches explored, every outcome triggered, full dossier coverage[/i]

[b]Orwell is a chilling, small-scale surveillance thriller that becomes far more unsettling the deeper you go.[/b]
Completing everything reveals a deceptively simple game that thrives on ambiguity, restraint, and moral discomfort.

You are the operator of Orwell, a government-run surveillance program that scrapes the internet, reads private messages, and compiles personal profiles. You do not break into buildings or interrogate suspects. You sift data, and what you choose to upload shapes the state’s understanding of events.

[b]Mechanically, the game is minimal but sharp.[/b]
Drag and drop datachunks into profiles. Cross-reference contradictions. Make judgment calls with limited context. A full completion run exposes how small decisions spiral into large consequences, often with no clear right answer.

[b]What makes Orwell work is how uncomfortably plausible it feels.[/b]
You start by targeting known suspects. But as the net widens, you begin to doubt your orders, your tools, and your own role. Completing every path shows the full range of outcomes, from quiet compliance to outright rebellion, and none of them are clean victories.

The visual design is slick and utilitarian. The writing carries the weight, offering just enough humanity to each character that invading their lives starts to feel like a violation.

Orwell does not shout its themes. It lets you live them.

The dystopian future is upon us. In it, we are tasked with examining all the various data about the target person - their communication, medical reports, posts on social sites, etc.; as all of the information can help us in protecting The Nation and its citizens.
When terror strikes in the heart of the capital, the [i]Orwell[/i] and we with it are put on the front line. With only one suspect at the beginning, we need to search throughout their data for any possible hints that could lead us to the truth about the attacks and the culprits behind them. But more suspects mean more information to get lost in and recognizing what info is relevant will put our deduction skills to a challenge. Also, anything inserted into [i]Orwell[/i] can't be taken back, and even the smallest information can cause a disaster.

Be prepared to read a lot in this game - there is tons of information and every new connection will add more to the ever-growing pile. You don't have to read everything if you don't feel like it, but if you do, you will know more. Simple as that. It can be quite enjoyable to peek into what people share about them on the internet… not very ethical from me, but when else would I have the opportunity? :P
The interface is simple - we are operating in a program that allows us to browse the internet, listen to phone conversations or control a suspect's PC/phone. From all of the information we pick up interesting data and attach it to the respective person. Some data will open new information sources, some are irrelevant or completely wrong, and some are in conflict with each other - from those we need to select the one we deem to be right. Those are the important ones that will influence how the story progress.

What bothered me was the fact that the phone calls can't be skipped or hastened in any way. So other runs for the remaining achievements were a little bit painful. Also, the replayability is somehow dubious - you can take a different approach and frame someone else, but otherwise it's still the same - you need to go through the same talks, lines, everything.

Although I am not much into political stuff and this is full of political talks, I have rather enjoyed it. Through Orwell you can firsthand experience how easily can information be twisted around… not that we don't know already in this age, right?

While the core concept is interesting, the game play and plot leave much to be desired. It is also incredibly short. The TLDR is that I would not recommend this unless the concept really grabs you.

The story revolves around a bombing and the activist group linked to it. You take the role of an investigator using social media, private messages/files and recorded phone calls to get to the bottom of everything. There seem to be a few possible different outcomes which could be interesting to explore if the people involved weren't so... stupid. I wont spoil anything but they basically make their own problems and then make bigger problems for themselves because they incorrectly think the bigger problems will solve their problems. It's like watching a train wreck in slow motion. It can be hard to get invested when you can't relate or empathise with the characters. I found myself thinking that most of them were horrible people who deserved what the plot threw at them.

The game play consists of reading through documents and chat logs and dragging over information that you determine to be relevant to the case. Some of this information is incorrect or contradictory and so you must vet information before committing it to the system. There are no taking information back even if you find contradicting information later on. This means a lot of your time will be spent going back and forward between different documents to pick out information and drag it to the appropriate file. This isn't exactly the most invigorating game play but when you are in the zone it can be somewhat enjoyable.

There isn't really much else to say. The game does have a political agenda and a underlying moral to it but it kind of falls on its face to the extent that I started to wonder if the resistant reading was the intended one.

While not the most exciting game, Orwell managed to keep me engaged and questioning until it's (amazing) ending. A well written, thoughtful puzzle game where your choices matter, and those choices are morally complex. It presents the pros and cons of the surveillance versus privacy issue, and gives you the freedom to choose where you stand on the matter rather than preaching at you.

I got this game for free, quite some time ago; But I never gave it the attention it deserves. The topics covered are very current and constantly debated. They generate controversy and distrust towards the authority itself.
Is it right to "spy" on the population in the name of security?
Is it right to authorize criminal actions based only on fragments of information or alleged crimes committed?
Is it right to use AI to track, follow and spy on people?
As you play Orwell, these questions will echo in your mind.
This game is inspired by the novel "1984" by Orwell.
You will find yourself behind a monitor of an advanced surveillance system and you will have to collect information on various people to "avoid" new crimes.
The gameplay is similar to a text adventure, where you have to read the information and decide which ones to load into the system. The interface is very simple and everything is explained very well at the beginning of the game.
The plot is very well developed and will hopefully raise some ethical questions about what you are doing.
This game is a little gem in a niche genre.
It is definitely worth playing.

For example, me failing to collect one particular piece of information changed the outcome, possibly drastically, at one point in the game. Would definitely recommend, especially when it's on sale and you can get a nice, short game for minimal cost.

What you do in this game : you are an investigator and you spy on people by using technology (including their personal devices and by listening to their conversations or reading their emails and texts). REVIEW

Pretty good short political sim game! I particularly liked the last hour of gameplay. It's not extremely fun and it can be a bit slow at times since you do read a lot of text, but it's fun enough for me to recommend the game. It's also pretty original and the story is interesting, so those 2 factors help a lot as well.

The concept of the game as a movie or a miniseries would work really well if you ask me. 

It's also a game that is good at making you realize that when you try to protect people by limiting freedom, not only does it not work well and takes resources, but it leads to a climate of fear, to injustice committed by the government AND to violence committed by some people whose freedom is being attacked. It is a game (fiction), but it does reflect past events and possible future events.

People just want to be free! Anyway... enjoy the game.

Some people say that the internet and social networks are the worst enemies of dictatorial regimes. But what if that’s not the case?
In Orwell, you will take on the role of an investigator working for the government. 
Your goal is to identify those responsible for a terrorist attack and to do so, you’ll have access to Orwell, a computer system capable of blurring the line between public and private information, allowing you to spy and, if you choose, condemn your suspects.

Primarily, the game involves selecting and collecting datachunks about your targets, which gradually unlock additional sources of information. These may offer useful clues or potentially lead you to an entirely different person. This process continues until at least one incriminating piece of evidence is discovered.

Pros:
[list]
[*]The game’s concept is quite unique
[*]Intuitive gameplay with investigative puzzles
[*]You can change the course of the events with your choices
[/list]


Cons:
[list]
[*]Very short, around 5 hours of gameplay
[*]Low replayability
[/list]

[b]Conclusion[/b]
If you enjoy investigative puzzle games and don’t mind reading walls of text, Orwell is a really interesting title, especially for its themes and ethical implications.
Its main downside is that it doesn’t last long, about 5 hour and the gameplay lacks variety, as most of the game mechanics are introduced within the first 15 minutes of gameplay.
I recommend it especially if it’s on sale.

First Playthrough: 

A short neat game experience with an interesting dystopian espionage theme. Simple and straight forward game mechanics kept my engagement high throughout the entire first run through of the game. Overall story was enthralling given the intrigue and mystery surrounding a web of individually well written characters that share a common "Thought". The usage of dramatic and impactful audio queues during moments of revelation help to sell the importance of key information to the story and make them memorable. 

Some negatives I find with this game is that in portions I tend to find myself feeling lost with what I should be looking for but the game does provide help icon hints to direct your attention to where you need to me, just sometimes those hints are not provided for every situation. Personally I find the ending to be a little too narrowing forcing you to choose between three separate paths and any of which leaves questions of the overall story unresolved unless you replay through the game till the end. This does encourage replayablity of at least three different experiences of the game, and with several side choices throughout, but still leaves a feeling, that after my first playthrough, doesn't leave me feeling completely satisfied.

Overall, for what the game is gunning to be, I'll give the experience an 8/10 despite my issues with the final act of the game.
